'''Jillian Beardwood''' (20 December 1934 – 28 October 2019)<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Beardwood, Jillian Elizabeth (1934–2019), mathematician and transport planner |url=https://www.oxforddnb.com/display/10.1093/ref:odnb/9780198614128.001.0001/odnb-9780198614128-e-90000380990 |access-date=2023-06-30 |website=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography |date=2023 |language=en |doi=10.1093/odnb/9780198614128.013.90000380990 |last1=Baker |first1=Anne Pimlott |isbn=978-0-19-861412-8 }}</ref> was a British mathematician known for the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley theorem.<ref name="totd">{{Cite web|url=https://www.theoremoftheday.org/OR/BHH/TotDBHH.pdf|title=The Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley Theorem}}</ref> Published by the [[Cambridge Philosophical Society]] in a 1959 article entitled "The Shortest Path Through Many Points",<ref name="auto">{{cite journal |last1=Beardwood |first1=Jillian |last2=Halton |first2=J. H. |last3=Hammersley |first3=J. M. |title=The shortest path through many points |journal=Mathematical Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society |date=October 1959 |volume=55 |issue=4 |pages=299–327 |doi=10.1017/S0305004100034095 |bibcode=1959PCPS...55..299B }}</ref> the [[theorem]] provides an [[Asymptotic analysis|asymptotic formula]] for the length of a [[travelling salesman problem|traveling salesperson tour]] of a given number of points in a [[unit square]], both in the [[worst case analysis|worst case]] and for random points.<ref name="totd" /><ref>Review of "The Shortest Path Through Many Points": S. J. Taylor, {{MR|0109316}}, {{zbl|0118.35601}}</ref>

==Early life==
Beardwood was born in [[Norwich]], England in 1934. After attending [[Sewell Park Academy|The Blyth School for Girls]], she studied mathematics at [[St. Hugh's College, Oxford]], earning [[British undergraduate degree classification#First-class honours|first-class honours]] and a [[master's degree]] in 1956.<ref name="X">{{cite news |last1=Beardwood |first1=Julia |title=Jillian Beardwood obituary |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2020/feb/06/jillian-beardwood-obituary |work=The Guardian |date=6 February 2020 }}</ref>

==Mathematics career==
After university, Beardwood accepted a position at the newly formed [[United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority]] (UKAEA), where she was one of four postgraduate students selected to study with [[John Hammersley]], a professor at [[Trinity College, Oxford]]. In that position, Beardwood gained access to the [[Ferranti Mercury]] computer at the UKAEA's research facility at [[Harwell Science and Innovation Campus|Harwell]], as well as to the [[ILLIAC II]] computer at the [[University of Illinois]]. She was later promoted to Senior Scientific Officer at the UKAEA, where she specialised in [[Monte Carlo method]]s and algorithms for modeling [[Complex geometry|complex geometrical situations]].<ref name="X" />

==The Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley Theorem==
The problem of determining the shortest closed path through a given set of n points is often called the "travelling salesman problem". A salesman, starting at and finally returning to his base, visits (n-1) other towns by the shortest possible route. If it is large, it may be prohibitively difficult to calculate the total mileages for each of the (n-1)! orders in which the towns may be visited, and to choose the smallest total.

As a practical substitute for an exact formula to determine the length of the shortest path, the Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley Theorem derived a simple asymptotic formula for the shortest length when n is large. The travelling salesman problem can involve either fixed or random points distributed over a certain region. The Theorem established that the shortest length between random points is asymptotically equal to a non-random function of n. For large n the distinction between the random and the non-random versions of the problem effectively vanishes. [[David Applegate|David L. Applegate]] described this in 2011 as a "famous result", and said "The remarkable theorem of Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley has received considerable attention in the research community, "with demonstrated uses in [[probability theory]], physics, [[operations research]] and [[computer science]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Applegate |first=D. |title=Traveling Salesman Problem |url={{GBurl|zfIm94nNqPoC|p=23}} |page=23}} Princeton, 2007</ref>

==Later career==
After leaving the UKAEA in 1968, Beardwood worked in transport modeling for the UK government's [[Transport Research Laboratory|Road Research Laboratory]]. In 1973, she joined the staff of the [[Greater London Council]] (GLC) where she directed the transport studies group until the GLC was dissolved in 1987. Her team helped to plan the [[M25 motorway|M25 orbital motorway]] around London and early [[congestion pricing]] systems. 

One of Beardwood's most cited studies for the GLC, "Roads Generate Traffic", found that highway construction encourages people to drive and leads to increased congestion.<ref name="Y">{{cite book |last1=Beardwood |last2=Elliott |first1=J. |first2=J. |chapter=Roads Generate Traffic |page=43 |title=Transport Policy: Proceedings of Seminar K Held at the PTRC Summer Annual Meeting, University of Sussex, England, from 15-18 July 1985 |date=1985 |publisher=PTRC Education and Research Services |isbn=978-0-86050-152-7 }}</ref><ref>[https://bettertransport.org.uk/sites/default/files/trunk-roads-traffic-report.pdf Trunk Roads and the Generation of Traffic] The Standing Advisory Committee on Trunk Road Assessment, p. 90</ref> "All that increases in road capacity do is allow people to abandon public transport in favour of the car".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mogridge |first1=Martin J. H. |title=Travel in Towns: Jam yesterday, jam today and jam tomorrow? |date=1990 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1-349-11798-7 |page=277 }}</ref> Beardwood's research accurately predicted that the M25 would quickly exceed its maximum capacity. It has been cited in support of policies encouraging the use of bicycles and other alternatives to cars.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lowe |first1=Marcia D. |title=The bicycle: Vehicle for a small planet |journal=Ekistics |date=1991 |volume=58 |issue=348/349 |pages=179–194 |jstor=43623194 }}</ref> Similarly, her later work included a study which predicted that the proposed [[East London River Crossing]] would quickly become congested if there were no significant routes available to provide relief.<ref name=":0" /> 

After the GLC's dissolution, Beardwood was employed in (and was a retained consultant to) the private sector, including for the transport planning consultancy MVA, Marcial Echenique and Partners Ltd and [[WSP Global|WSP]] Group. She also worked in academic posts, as a senior research fellow at the [[London School of Economics]] and as a lecturer in transport planning at the [[Polytechnic of Central London]] (1989–90).<ref name=":0" />
